questions.question_text: For a normally distributed dataset, what percentage of scores lie within $1$ standard deviation of the mean?

options.why: Halved the band, giving only the part between the mean and $\mu+\sigma$.
Added the $50\%$ below the mean to the $34\%$ above it, which gives everything below $\mu+\sigma$.
Gave the tail beyond one standard deviation instead of the band within it.

questions.question_text: For a normally distributed dataset, what percentage of scores lie between the mean and $3$ standard deviations above the mean?

options.why: Quoted the whole band within three standard deviations without halving it.
Gave the tail beyond $\mu+3\sigma$ instead of the region from the mean up to it.
Assumed every score above the mean lies within three standard deviations.

questions.question_text: For a normally distributed dataset, what percentage of scores are more than $2$ standard deviations below the mean?

options.why: Left the whole leftover $100\% - 95\% = 5\%$ in one tail instead of halving it between the two tails.
Gave the band between $\mu-3\sigma$ and $\mu-2\sigma$ instead of the whole tail below $\mu-2\sigma$.
Gave the region from the mean down to $\mu-2\sigma$ rather than the region beyond it.

questions.question_text: For a normally distributed dataset, what percentage of scores lie between $1$ and $3$ standard deviations above the mean?

options.why: Used $99.7\% - 68\%$, which includes the matching band below the mean as well.
Added the $16\%$ tail beyond $\mu+\sigma$ to $49.85\%$ instead of subtracting the $34\%$.
Gave the whole region from the mean to $\mu+3\sigma$ without removing the first standard deviation.

questions.question_text: For a normally distributed dataset, what percentage of scores are less than $2$ standard deviations above the mean?

options.why: Gave the band within two standard deviations, leaving out everything below $\mu-2\sigma$.
Gave only the region from the mean up to $\mu+2\sigma$, omitting the $50\%$ below the mean.
Gave the tail above $\mu+2\sigma$ instead of everything below it.

questions.question_text: For a normally distributed dataset, what percentage of scores lie between $3$ standard deviations below the mean and $1$ standard deviation above the mean?

options.why: Used $50\%$ for the region below the mean instead of the $49.85\%$ that reaches only to $\mu-3\sigma$.
Used the $16\%$ tail above $\mu+\sigma$ instead of the $34\%$ between the mean and $\mu+\sigma$.
Added the $0.15\%$ tail below $\mu-3\sigma$ to $34\%$ instead of the $49.85\%$ inside it.

questions.question_text:
The lifetimes of a brand of light globe are normally distributed with a mean of $1200$ hours and a standard deviation of $60$ hours.
What percentage of globes last between $1080$ and $1140$ hours?

options.why: Used the band between $\mu-3\sigma$ and $\mu-2\sigma$ instead of the band between $\mu-2\sigma$ and $\mu-\sigma$.
Used $95\% - 68\%$, which counts the matching band above the mean as well.
Gave the region from the mean down to $1140$ hours instead of the band between $1080$ and $1140$ hours.

questions.question_text: The masses of packets of rice are normally distributed with a mean of $500$ g. About $99.7\%$ of packets have a mass between $476$ g and $524$ g. Find the standard deviation.

options.why: Treated $476$ g and $524$ g as two standard deviations from the mean instead of three.
Divided the full width $524 - 476 = 48$ by $3$ instead of dividing the half-width $24$ by $3$.
Took the half-width from the mean as the standard deviation without dividing by $3$.

questions.question_text:
Scores on a video game are normally distributed with a mean of $640$ and a standard deviation of $45$.
One player scores $730$.
Which statement best describes this score?

options.text: It is $2$ standard deviations above the mean, and only about $2.5\%$ of scores are higher, so it is unusual.
It is $2$ standard deviations above the mean, and about $5\%$ of scores are higher, so it is unusual.
options.why: Left the whole leftover $100\% - 95\% = 5\%$ in the upper tail instead of halving it between the two tails.

options.text: It is $2$ standard deviations above the mean, and about $47.5\%$ of scores are higher, so it is not unusual.
options.why: Used the region from the mean up to $\mu+2\sigma$ instead of the region beyond $\mu+2\sigma$.

options.text: It is $2$ standard deviations above the mean, and about $95\%$ of scores are higher, so it is not unusual.
options.why: Quoted the percentage lying within two standard deviations as if it were the percentage above $730$.

questions.question_text: In the standard normal distribution, what is the approximate value of $P(-1<Z<1)$?

options.why: The interval omits both tails beyond one standard deviation.
The central interval contains more than half of the standard Normal distribution.
The standard Normal distribution is fully specified by its definition.

questions.solution_text: For a standard Normal variable, approximately $68.3\%$ of observations lie within one standard deviation of the mean. Thus $P(-1<Z<1)\approx0.68$, represented by $2/3$ among the options.
